title: The Cambridge Ghost Club, from Dickens to 2026
excerpt: Emer Afram speaks to the current Chairman of Cambridge's Ghost Club about the past, present, and future of paranormal investigation in Cambridge
content:
Emer Afram speaks to the current Chairman of Cambridge’s Ghost Club about the past, present, and future of paranormal investigation in Cambridge

by

“The Ghosts have it,” wrote William Howitt to Charles Dickens in 1859, relaying the conclusion of “a Society, jocularly called the Ghost-Club, consisting of a number of Cambridge men… whose object has been thoroughly to sift this question of apparitions”. Howitt described a group of Trinity College fellows meeting in 1855 to study and test the paranormal in Cambridge and beyond, combining metaphysics and spiritual practices in an intellectual pursuit of truth. ​

This club has prevailed, dissolving and reforming many times since its conception, currently composed of 400 members who come together for meetings, investigations, and social events. But has its approach changed? How does today’s Ghost Club compare to the coven of academics? Has our engagement with the spiritual world shifted? ​

“A Society, jocularly called the Ghost-Club, consisting of a number of Cambridge men”

In 1863, George Cruikshank mocked the newly established London ‘Ghost Club’ in his pamphlet, ‘A Discovery Concerning Ghosts with a Rap at the Rapper’, a series of caricatures depicting ghost investigations, such as a probe into whether a ghost must be thin and scraggy, or is permitted to hold some extra weight. Despite teasing from sceptics and papers, the group conducted itself seriously; a male-only, private members’ club with big names like Dickens himself, who investigated strange goings-on, including the Davenport Brothers. The group’s next iteration is perhaps most accurate to its foundations, as it enjoyed a close but fleeting relationship with the Society for Psychical Research, reconciling the nebulous world of spirits with hard, empirical evidence. ​

Crossing through the veil of the 1900s, Siegfried Sasoon and W.B. Yeats joined the ranks, attracting coverage from The Times, which, although still sceptical, reports on the activities of the group, including one dinner in 1947 promising £1000 to anyone who could prove the disappearing rope trick attended by the Bishop of London. It may be hard to commune these writers of fiction and holy men with the serious study of metaphysics which had been foundational in Cambridge all those years prior. And certainly the group blended into the overtly theatrical Edwardian spirituality, with its aesthetic of mysticism and eastern philosophies a wispy backdrop for focused research. Yet, the pursuit of truth was still primordial, with Yeats delivering a rousing lecture about ghosts and dreams. While self-indulgent in content, it included the hard ‘fact’ that 4/5s of mediums are unreliable, and cheats – but we should still acknowledge the truthful ones. ​

“One dinner in 1947 promising £1000 to anyone who could prove the disappearing rope trick attended by the Bishop of London”

The Club’s operations wavered with what was spiritually in vogue, and as investigations became more clinical in the 20th century, it dissolved for just eighteen months in 1936 with an order to seal the records in the British Library. Today, the Ghost Club has perhaps lost some of the mystique of Edwardian smoke and mirrors, but its commitment to uncovering the paranormal is unwavering. ​

I caught up with Alan Murdie – barrister, author, ghost hunter and the current Chairman – to ascertain the Club’s place in 2026. ​

Murdie describes the society as “a cultural body which celebrates our unique British traditions of ghosts and hauntings but also seeks to explore the topic and the possibility of survival after death in a serious and non-judgmental way, enabling involvement by both sceptics and believers in a neutral setting”. This smacks of the Trinity fellows’ investigations, as stated by Sir William Barrett in the 1932 Journal of the Society for Psychical Research: “interested in spectral appearances before or after death, apparitions of all kinds,” topics that Mr Murdie says the club is still aligned with.

Whilst today’s Ghost Club is a democratically run non-profit organisation, with membership available upon application, it seems not so far removed from the 1855 iteration. But how has it changed? ​

“Whilst today’s Ghost Club is a democratically run non-profit organisation, it seems not so far removed from the 1855 iteration”

When I think of ghosts, I see white bedsheets with holes cut out, franchises such as The Conjuring or Paranormal Activity, the rattling window in my first-year staircase which let in screeching wind, and Jim Morrison’s Parisian grave. None of these are particularly serious, and you could argue they are influenced by the commercial. In Cambridge, our view of the paranormal is also largely that of a consumer: we get a tarot reading at May Balls, are approached by street hawkers offering to read our futures, and share stories of allegedly haunted colleges. ​

I asked Murdie if he believes this ‘pop-spirituality’ has changed how the club is perceived. He disagreed, stating that the effects of entertainment are “generally short-lived” and “over-sensational”. He highlighted the media’s treatment of the 1977-9 Enfield Poltergeist case, which was investigated by two Ghost Club members who had a much better appreciation of the details, given the “scientific, philosophical and spiritual methods” used. ​

I then asked where Murdie sees the group in 10 years. He was and optimistic and mentioned a range of fields that can lend themselves to paranormal scholarship: “psychology, medicine, physics, geology, biology, folklore, archaeology, history, the social sciences, as well as parapsychology and psychical research.” Murdie hopes that in the coming years, a new generation of parapsychologists and doctoral students will get involved, particularly in examining hauntings outside of Europe and North America.​

“Current Chairman Murdie’s favourite ghost story concerns a pair of doomed lovers in Corpus Christi”

Let us return to the original circle in Cambridge, where ghosts surely outnumber the living in ancient colleges. How has spirituality endured within our city’s walls? ​

Murdie founded and ran the Cambridge Ghost Walks from 1999 to 2007. When asked if he perceived a change in audience, he said no. The Walks consistently attracted people from a wide range of ages and backgrounds, and he noted merely a shortening of attention spans. ​Perhaps, our approach to the paranormal is not so dissimilar to that expressed in 19th-century Trinity College.

Murdie’s favourite Cambridge ghost story concerns a pair of doomed lovers in Corpus Christi College, where the Master’s daughter Catherine fell in love with a student called James. One night, when met with her father’s explosive disapproval, Catherine was forced to hide James in a cupboard – a cupboard he never left alive. Catherine died a few months later, either of a broken heart or by jumping from the roof of Old Court. After dark, the pair’s footsteps are said to be heard running around college and echoing off the surrounding flagstone pavements. ​

The next time you’re around King’s Parade, see if you can hear them reunite beyond the veil.
